thread.title: Iowa House passes property tax bill, no deal made yet with Senate - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: Iowa House passes property tax bill, no deal made yet with Senate - NewsBreak

author: Teodora Mitov
title: Iowa House passes property tax bill, no deal made yet with Senate - NewsBreak
text:
By Teodora Mitov ,
1 hours ago
DES MOINES, Iowa — Republicans say a property tax deal is close after state representatives voted to advance the House GOP property tax proposal on Wednesday.
The Senate passed its property tax bill, Senate File 2472 , a couple of weeks ago. This week, the bill was amended to include language from the “compromise bill” Speaker Pat Grassley (R- New Hartford) briefed reporters on last week.
The bill, managed by Representative Carter Nordman (R-Panora), includes a 2% cap on local government revenue growth, including new construction and excluding debt service levies and school funding.
Story continues below
It would also limit local government reserve accounts to 35% of budgets and create a new restricted reserve account for local governments to use to budget for large capital projects and public safety above the 35%.
To provide residential property tax relief, the bill would eliminate the turn the Homestead Tax Credit into a tax exemption. Homeowners would not pay property taxes on the first $15,000 of their home’s value. The tax credit for seniors, veterans, and disabled populations would not change. However, the bill does not include a property tax freeze for seniors, unlike previous proposals.
The current state funding that supports the Homestead Tax Credit would go to reducing the $5.40 school tax levy to $5.00.
To address assessment and valuation, the GOP plan would shift the burden of proof to assessors if assessments rise more than 10% over two years.
Representative Nordman said the plan would make local governments accountable for property taxes. In his closing remarks, he said, “For too long, our property tax system has put certainty for government budgets over the certainty of family budgets. Today we flip that script… We are simply asking for the same fiscal discipline from our governments that our citizens practice every day.”
When asked by reporters if property taxes for Iowans will decrease next year under this plan, Nordman said that was the intent of the bill. He said, “It also takes local government accountability. In a perfect world, the legislature has nothing to do with property taxes. These are local decisions that are being made, but we have seen that property taxes have gotten so out of control in this state, the legislature has to step in and put guardrails up with caps and other things that we’re doing.”
Democrats criticized the bill, saying it would not provide relief for taxpayers. Representative Larry McBurney (D- Urbandale) pointed to House File 718 from 2023, which included a 3% revenue cap and did not result in property tax relief for Iowans.
McBurney said, “The problem isn’t the cap. The problem continues to be that assessments continue to rise, and I don’t care if it’s 2%, 3%, if the value of your property is going up, you will never lower your levy fast enough to be able to truly lower property taxes in this state.”
Representative Aime Wichtendahl (R- Hiawatha) said the bill would force local governments to finance more debts.
“With the hard cap of 2% and the constitutionally protected debt service levy at 5%, what this bill will do is force local governments to finance more debt to maintain the current level of services. So, then the property taxes that our residents are paying, those property tax increases, and they are now paying interest on it,” said Wichtendahl.
Nordman said the plan would provide roughly $450 million in relief for taxpayers starting next year and $4 billion in relief over the next six years. However, he says local governments play important roles in how and if taxpayers will see this relief.
“There’s different classification, there’s different assessments. Every local government is different. Counties are different, the cities are different, your extensions are different, your community colleges are different. Every community the way they tax is different. So, it’s not just going to be a straight divide that number by the amount of homes,” Nordman told reporters. “It does take buy in from the local governments to also try to provide property tax relief alongside this.”
Ultimately, representatives voted mostly along party lines to pass the bill. Representatives Sean Bagniewski (D- Des Moines), Dan Gosa (D- Davenport), and Kenan Judge (D- Waukee) voted with Republicans in favor of the plan.
House Democrats released their own amendment, which is identical to the plan they introduced before the session started. They said the plan would provide immediate relief for taxpayers, unlike proposals the GOP has introduced.
The majority party voted against this amendment and Nordman said the Democrats’ plan was “unsustainable” and provided “short-term solutions.”
The bill now heads back to the Senate. Speaker Grassley told reporters last week that this bill is not the final version and he expects the Senate to make changes.
Senator Dan Dawson (R- Council Bluffs) led the Senate GOP in property tax discussions. Following the House vote, Dawson said, “We have been clear on our position, and we continue to maintain that a conversation on the type of property tax relief Iowans want includes diversifying revenue streams, simplifying the system, and bringing the substantial relief Iowa homeowners need.”
Senate Majority Leader Mike Klimesh (R- Spillville) said, “The Senate has passed our vision for true property tax reform. Now that a version has passed the Iowa House, I am optimistic we can work on a compromise that includes aspects of all our plans, helps address the fact that Iowa is the one of the worst states for property tax burdens, and provides relief to the Iowans desperately asking for it.”
